speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's next phase of development towards a Smart Nation has opened up many exciting developments in terms of jobs and business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I recall the times in this Chamber when Members, such as Ms Jessica Tan, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and I, spoke about how the engineering and technology fields have become less attractive professions in recent years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 2014, the number of technology talents in tech startups was about 33,000.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, it is important that the Government develops a clear manpower strategy to maximise our local talent pool who are keen to develop a career in ICT.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important to develop our manpower both in depth, for them to specialise and get certified in new exciting fields, and balance their development with a breadth of soft skills in areas of leadership, business management, functional design, creativity as well as sales and marketing, to differentiate our educated workforce from those of other low-cost countries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, we are only competing on costs, which depresses salaries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the top end, it is also important that we produce ICT and business leaders who can compete on the international stage, given competition from other tech powerhouses here in Asia, such as Korea, China, India and Japan.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important that we build a world-renowned brand for our ICT workforce as innovators and being able to apply quickly the latest technology can offer.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a small nation, we may not always be at the forefront of invention, but it is important that we are able to be creative in the application of the best technologies from the world over and be able to leverage Singapore as a testbed to implement new ideas and market them effectively all over the world.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over the next few years, I hope that the Ministry will do its utmost to attract more Singaporean students and workers into the ICT profession to ride on its growth for the years to come.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The challenged economy today presents an opportunity for the ICT sector to attract those outside the ICT profession with an aptitude for technology, especially many middle-aged professionals, who may find themselves displaced as the economy restructures to fuel this growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we embark on the Smart Nation, we must move quickly to ensure that our Singaporean workforce is ready with the skillsets and mindset to exploit the opportunities to come.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This puts many other industrial and tech parks under the spotlight too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Understandably, one may question whether we should retain such sectors if few Singaporeans are keen to take on jobs there.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Understandably, these roles usually support the region, or even the world.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, their working hours may be shift-based and because of its back-office nature, the salaries may be at the lower end of the scale.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But before we judge which jobs should be retained or moved out, we must recognise that it is not just about high-value jobs or jobs that Singaporeans want.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The whole ICT ecosystem must be aligned for us to continue to attract leading technology firms to set up here.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we swing too much to the extreme and move these perceived low-value operations, such as data centres, support operations, out of Singapore – we risk losing many high-value jobs too because the whole ecosystem is inter-dependent.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the enabling nature of ICT, companies across various industries are also dependent on these operations, particularly companies that serve the region or the world, including banks, logistics and manufacturing firms.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The revenue stream for many local and international ICT firms, including the leading brands, also rely on the international hubs here for business.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, if these firms lose clients because of fewer ICT infrastructure and operations being based here, we lose a strong justification to retain the headquarters of these firms here.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If this happens, we could lose more high-value jobs in the ICT sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I would like to hear from the Ministry on how it plans to balance our dependency on foreign manpower, while channelling our local manpower towards building a strong Singapore Core in ICT firms, and ICT professions that support our businesses and Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Singapore becomes more and more digitally connected and moves towards the age of sensors and the Internet of Things, securing our cyber space, devices and personal data becomes ever more important.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does the Ministry rate the awareness of cyber security among individuals and businesses here in Singapore as well as the steps they are taking to keep the data secure?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, cybersecurity is not just about reputational risk.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The risk to operations, even denial of access to public services, is possible if hackers take control of our critical infrastructure, not to mention, the mischief and safety risks that could be caused to our transport, defence systems and confidential Government information.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Imagine if a hacker is able to take control of our train system, air traffic control or even poison our water by changing the chlorine composition of our water tanks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I mentioned in my Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) cut that we need to be ready for "hybrid warfare", where our businesses and critical infrastructure may be targeted by cyberattacks to cripple our economy and business confidence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To complement the technology and risk initiatives, we must also have strong legal frameworks to tackle different forms of cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, we have the Computer Misuse and Cybersecurity Act.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are our cyber laws sufficient to handle cyber terrorism, and emerging platforms, such as blockchains?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Attacks may also come from foreign state and non-state entities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was well-attended by students, employers and mid-career professionals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Students wanted to know if they could continue upgrading their skills in ICT after they leave IHLs, given the constant developments in the ICT industry, and if they could aspire to C-suite level jobs, given their technical backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers shared their immediate needs and requirement for industry-ready talent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mid-career professionals from adjacent industries to ICT wanted to cross over in the quickest and most painless fashion.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the need to develop local talent so as to enable the healthy and sustainable development of the Smart Nation initiative as well as deal with cybersecurity concerns, how would the Ministry address local manpower development to address the concerns of the various groups I mentioned?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are we doing this in the most resource-efficient and timely manner?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even though female representation in our ICT workforce is higher than that, say, in the United States (US), how are we making ICT education attractive to female students given the rising importance of the industry and the availability of good jobs?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are good role models like Jenny Lee of GGV Capital who has made a name for herself as an ICT venture capitalist with a Midas touch.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we leverage more on the positive influence of such female thought leaders?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, while company-led training programmes and internships are the best way to ensure skills fit to job requirements, not all companies may have the resources to devote time and manpower to training.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In December last year, the Ukrainian power supply was shut down by a cyberattack for six hours and, more than two months after the cyberattack, the power grid's central control is still not fully operational.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Separately, in February this year, hackers attempted to steal almost $1 billion from the Central Bank of Bangladesh.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: State and trade secrets have been the target of hacking and cyberattacks in recent years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The perpetrators, whether state-sponsored or criminal groups, aimed to cause disruption to key systems for strategic reasons, ransom, theft and to make political points.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: According to FireEye, a global cybersecurity company, cyberattacks are being increasingly mounted on Southeast Asian countries, due to interest in the region's growing industry sectors, such as energy, telecommunications, high-tech, transportation and finance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Territorial disputes in the South China Sea are also driving cyber espionage activities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we move towards greater connectivity via our Smart Nation programme, different sectors with various expertise in cybersecurity will be plugged into the system – Government, power, land transport, maritime, civil aviation, water, security emergency, health, banking and finance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not all sectors have networks built in with security in mind.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, many sectors may not have designed security into their networks as they were built.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How does the Cyber Security Agency (CSA) intend to work with all the different sectors in Singapore to ensure that they are resilient against cyberattacks and, as such, ensure the resiliency of the nation?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How are we doing this by design as we progress the Smart Nation initiative?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, given the international aspects of cybersecurity, with attacks either mounted or routed through other countries, how is CSA promoting cooperation with other international bodies, so that there is an aligned and concerted effort to guide against cyber threats?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had spoken about the hacking of the Bank of Bangladesh's accounts in New York during the Ministry of Defence's (MINDEF) Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Attempts were made to squirrel out almost $1 billion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If hackers can target bank accounts in New York, they will likely have the capability to target banks and other IT infrastructure in other parts of the world, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand that the Cyber Security Agency (CSA) has been set up to build up capabilities and to respond to cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: CSA brings together Government agencies as well major players in critical sectors such as energy, banking, and financial sectors, and other critical parts of our infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: How does CSA ensure that these critical sectors are prepared for cyber threats?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are mid-career professionals who may be willing to explore the possibility of switching careers and joining other sectors and some may even be from the retrenched group.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If possible, can the Minister also share his plans to prepare our young for the pre-infocomm sector and make it even more enticing?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Go further beyond that and you could argue that at the heart of every successful script is an engaging and well-told story.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recall the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) previously announcing that it would develop a Creators' Space to nurture the digital film and video sub-sectors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on this Creators' Space and also what is being done to enhance the quality of idea generation, storytelling and scriptwriting in the media industry?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Much has been said by the Members of this House about readying our economy and people for the future and about encouraging a spirit of partnership, care and resilience.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They centre on the themes of "partnership" and "transformation".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The single most important issue facing the media sector today in Singapore and the world, is convergence.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Convergence is the merging of media like print, television, radio with the Internet and with portable and interactive technology, and this has transformed the way information is created, distributed and consumed globally.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This throws up many opportunities as well as challenges for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The 2016 Budget, in my opinion, addresses many of the issues brought on by convergence and I am heartened by the Government's foresight and support.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us know that countries, such as China and India, are spearheading the growth of the infocomm sector globally, both in technology and talent.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They bring new technologies to market faster, and many talented individuals from overseas are now in Singapore running and working in small and medium enterprises (SMEs) as well as large companies.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a bad thing, as we can, indeed learn, and improve by working with top talent.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has done much to manage this sensitive area while ensuring a global business-friendly ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But it is still far too common for us in the media industry to see companies flying in individuals from overseas to take on lead roles in big projects and initiatives, when these positions could have been filled by capable, homegrown talent.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I strongly urge the Government to consider further fine-tuning its approach to the accessibility of Singapore jobs to talent from overseas.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Where local and highly capable talent already exist in that particular sector, then Singaporeans should be given first priority.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We must encourage a talent ecosystem where local and international companies which prioritise Singaporean talent see the benefits of being our partners for growth, and transform, over time, into commercial pillars for the local community.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government must take the lead in setting this tone, those in positions of leadership and influence must themselves make a conscious effort to mentor homegrown executives.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans are not just highly efficient in functional roles.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans today can be truly exceptional in leadership and management roles.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: For if we do not make hiring our own people a priority in Singapore-funded projects, then who will?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: A key recommendation by the committee then was to strengthen and enhance local vibrancy of original content.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Viewing patterns on local TV have stabilised, with Suria, Vasantham and Channel NewsAsia growing their viewership.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Programmes like "Wild City" and "Food Empire", just to name two, on Channel NewsAsia, are getting rave reviews here and overseas.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The increase in funding and the use of specialised foreign expertise have resulted in strong local TV productions. "Tanglin", a daily drama series on Channel 5, is my personal favourite.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the steady TV ratings, the online viewership has been very extremely encouraging.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Its local stories, multiracial cast, fresh talent and good production values make the stories very watchable.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Cable broadcaster StarHub has also recently joined the fray and is also commissioning projects to independent production companies as a result of the contestable funding initiative.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: These funds are absolutely crucial to the survival and growth of our independent production community and will be a lifeline in a period of slowing economic growth.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Feedback from the production community has been for more transparency with regard to budgets and quotas.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Government could consider making public the projects that are commissioned under the PSB framework, from Mediacorp as well as from the independent production companies, including details like durations and production budgets.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This will create greater transparency in the marketplace.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It will also create more goodwill and trust between the broadcasters and the production community.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Just five years ago, South Korean platforms used to buy most of the available American and overseas content, be it drama or lifestyle shows.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Today, South Korean companies invest almost totally in local, original content, mainly drama and K-pop, that have become highly popular at home and, increasingly, around the world.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: At a global television market in Cannes, France, last week, the South Koreans were trying to sell distributors, such as myself, content and formats for distribution in the American and European markets.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is a reversal and, indeed, a transformation of the industry.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Convergence has resulted in greater variety and, with it, greater expectations of high-quality content.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We must, as an industry, become better at mentoring our homegrown talent, particularly in the areas of production and commissioning.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We must also become better at facilitating the transition of our SME production companies from local set-ups to international players.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The Media Development Authority (MDA) was one of the pioneer Government agencies in the region that embarked on industry development initiatives.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Today, homegrown outfits, like The Moving Visuals Company and Beach House Pictures, are regional and global players, doing work for broadcasters like Discovery and National Geographic.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: More can be done to encourage the spirit of adventure among our local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mentorship programmes too can be tweaked to better match experienced international mentors with local talent.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: For example, a young, quirky Singaporean producer I met recently was matched with a mentor from the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While this could conceptually result in something interesting, a lot could also be lost in translation between genres and generations.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: She would have been better suited for a mentor from a younger skewing channel, perhaps like Channel 4.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mediapolis@one-north is Singapore's first digital media hub, where emerging media technologies, content, services and applications are being developed, produced, financed and distributed to the world.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is not yet complete, but is already facing rising competition from our neighbours and beyond.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The jewel in that crown is Pinewood Studios.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It has world-class facilities designed for major productions.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The most important attraction of Iskandar, however, is the financial incentive.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mediapolis in Singapore boasts world-class facilities as well.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: More effort should be made in raising the profile of Mediapolis and celebrating its advantages and successes.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, local companies could also be incentivised to use the facilities more regularly.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In the last few years, I have also noticed that Singapore has a more muted presence in international conventions —

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram
text: In summary, Mdm Chair, challenges notwithstanding, I laud and support the Government's efforts and provisions in the Budget that will help the media sector transform itself for future challenges.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The hardware market segment grew fastest during this period, at 19.4%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The second fastest growing market segment was that for software/IT services, growing less than half as fast, at just under 9%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This was followed by telecommunications, which grew at 6.5% and, finally, content activities, which grew slowest at 5.6%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The proportions of revenue contributed by the remaining segments have all either remained flat or shrunk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although good performance in the hardware segment is a good thing, the question I have is whether and to what extent the software and infocomm services segments are being affected by the lack of required manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although employment in infocomm has not grown as quickly as in some other sectors, the compound annual growth rate of 4.9% between 2001 and 2014 has been very healthy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At end-2014, infocomm accounted for 3.3% of overall employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This was almost unchanged from 2011, when the proportion stood at 3%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In 2015, infocomms was the third fastest growing sector in the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Its expansion of 4.2% was more than twice that of the overall economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The manpower crunch appears to have been casting a long shadow over the future prospects of growth in our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If the problem lies with the preference of Singaporean workers, it may be possible to make the jobs more attractive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, many jobs in the ICT sector should not be considered unattractive by virtue of their standing in the technological hierarchy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If the reason for their lack of appeal is because they are technically demanding, then we must have a serious and deep-seated problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is the problem also to do with limits in the supply of local manpower?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In the meantime, what can be done to prevent the manpower shortage from permanently diminishing the potential for the ICT sector?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is a good sign of the progress of the Smart Nation initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We have clearly achieved an Internet infrastructure whose quality is up to the demands of a Smart Nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But are we exploiting this infrastructure mainly just for consumption?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: How much of the capacity of this world-class infrastructure is actually being employed to drive our technological development?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What is being done to encourage software and content development to ride on our magnificent Internet infrastructure?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The relatively weak performance in the infocomm industry of the software and services segments compared to the hardware segment appears to suggest that the excellent infrastructure that has been built for Internet connectivity is not being exploited to its fullest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Can more be done to motivate our population to move beyond mere consumption of content towards making a greater impact as developers in areas, such as Internet gaming, marketing platforms and content provision?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Ms Sun Xueling and Assoc Prof Randolph Tan also observed this, and they asked how we can prevent ICT manpower shortages and in particular, reduce our reliance on foreign manpower in certain ICT sub-sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As demand far outstrips current supply and because the landscape is changing so rapidly, it is difficult to meet company needs for skilled manpower without non-Singaporeans entirely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: But we must do our best to support our Singaporeans to be highly skilled so that they can compete with global talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Hence, today, I will talk about how we will do more to accelerate infocomm capability development and build a strong Singapore Core for infocomm media.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We must also ensure that our students have work-ready skills and our current workers in the sector can easily renew their skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To build the future pipeline of infocomm professionals, we must start young.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Hence, we launched the Code@SG movement in 2014 to nurture interest in technology among our young.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will continue to develop coding and computational thinking as a national capability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Next, Madam, we will focus on the 6,000 or so students from each cohort, who are already in infocomm disciplines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Today, our estimates indicate that a significant proportion of them do not enter the sector upon graduation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Infocomm Development Authority (IDA) has studied this together with the stakeholders and one reason is that employers are looking for applicants with strong experience, even prior to graduation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: So, we will launch an Industry Preparation for Pre-Graduates Programme (iPREP).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: IDA will work with IHLs to select students and place them on this structured internship and mentorship programme, so that they can build their portfolios and gain sufficient entry-level skills and experience even before they graduate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This will help more young Singaporeans like Tan Kai Heng, an NTU Computer Science alumnus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: During his internship at Gametize, he worked with a dynamic team and even co-led to develop an Android app from scratch.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The internship helped him become a confident software developer and he was subsequently offered a job with Gametize upon graduation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He has been with them for almost four years now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will do more to support our working ICT professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We currently co-fund company-led training (CLT) programmes with industry partners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, Google has partnered IDA to roll out the Squared Data Analytics Programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Vicnan Pannirselvam, a graduate in Philosophy, Politics and Economics, wanted to pursue a data-related career.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: After the training, he was deployed to TBWA, an international advertising agency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There, he gained practical experience in integrating data with advertising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He did so well that he was offered a job as a Data Strategist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Celestine Goh found that the programme helped to open doors for trainees like her to access a large community of like-minded individuals and mentors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: She also developed her skills and gained valuable experience there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: She is now a Data and Analytics Specialist at Maxus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mid-level professionals will now also benefit from the local and overseas training and attachments to build expertise and competencies for jobs in demand, especially in emerging areas like cybersecurity and analytics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will also help experienced professionals deepen their skills or convert to new infocomm disciplines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: IDA's Critical Infocomm Technology Resource Programme (CITREP) helps approximately 3,000 mid-level professionals take up professional short courses and certifications every year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Moving forward, we will expand the CITREP+ programme and also help entry level professionals to start acquiring ICT skills and professional certifications early in their careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about our efforts to help non-infocomm mid-career professionals make a career switch and join the infocomm sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Participants are taught through industry projects by industry practitioners, receive career support and have job placement opportunities with potential employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will ramp up the capacity for such accelerated Tech Immersion and Placement programmes, to support more than 1,000 Singaporean trainees over the next three years, especially those with Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) backgrounds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will work very closely with industry to grow this into our flagship platform where all Singapore ICT professionals can receive training and career advice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The infocomm industry associations – Singapore IT Federation, Singapore Computer Society and the IT Management Association – have already played a huge role in the past to develop the National Infocomm Competency Framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These associations, Madam, will continue to define new competencies under the TechSkills Accelerator, and support our shift towards greater recognition of skills mastery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will also provide funding support to Singaporeans who use the platform to validate their skills A new feature of the TechSkills Accelerator is that the partnership will be anchored by major employers in the sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This is important because employers must also themselves want to develop a strong Singapore Core and offer competitive remuneration to recognise skills achievement and not just paper qualifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I encourage more companies to come on board and to put more emphasis in talent development, so that we can together build a strong Singapore core for infocomm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked about how we can encourage more Singaporeans, especially our young, to create more content.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I am pleased to share that, this year, MDA will expand on its efforts to help enhance the capacity of the media sector to create new content for new platforms, so that we can transform the media sector to be future-ready.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I previously announced that we would launch a Creators' Space at Pixel Building in one-north.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It is on track to start operations by the end of this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Key partners, such as Adobe, digital creative brand NewMedia, online video platform Dailymotion and Disney's Maker Studios, the global leader in online short-form videos, have been confirmed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will take it one step further, by running other initiatives related to content development at Creators' Space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In this way, we will enable synergies between professionals in the various media sub-sectors and create a truly vibrant space for learning, experimentation and collaboration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: One of the initiatives that will leverage the Creators' Space is Story Lab.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Darryl David asked how we can improve the quality of film, video and TV, especially in the area of idea generation and content creation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Our Story Lab initiative helps to enhance the creative capacity of our media industry to develop compelling story ideas and innovative ways to tell these stories across various media platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Just last month, we ran a "Game Writing versus Narrative Design Masterclass", in partnership with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and the National Book Development Council (NBDC).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: About 40 media and literary professionals came together to learn about game writing techniques and tools to develop game stories.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will launch more programmes later this year, such as the WritersLab, to hone scriptwriting for television.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For the film sector, programmes such as the Chinese scriptwriting with local film producer mm2 Entertainment has indeed been very successful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: They brought in notable Hong Kong and Taiwan writers as mentors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This programme will help our promising local screenwriters develop deeper script writing skills, to better serve the Mandarin-speaking market in the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The games sub-sector is one of the fastest growing media sectors in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: GSC offers budding game developers mentorship programmes, support for them to take their business and ideas overseas as well as business networking and access to financing opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Many of our game developers have made their mark, both locally and internationally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For instance, Rotten Mage's Spacejacked won the Best Linux Game award at Intel's Level Up 2015 game developer contest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Another game, Autumn Dynasty Warlords by Touch Dimensions, was among the top grossing strategy games on iTunes Store in several countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These two games are among many that grew out of GSC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The co-location of the Story Lab and GSC with Creators' Space will be a significant step to help our Singapore media companies become even more independently competitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It will help facilitate collaboration between various media sub-sectors to bring about richer consumer experiences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, game developers today use data to better understand their consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This capability can be shared more widely to other media professionals, so that they can develop more innovative ways to commercialise their content.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I am confident, Madam, that when the Creators' Space opens later this year, we will inspire more Singaporeans to create original content for consumers not only in Singapore, but around the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We also believe that it is essential that these sectors develop a strong Singapore Core of talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will succeed, if we can attract more Singaporeans with a passion for their craft.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: People like Fadli bin Sidek, whom I met earlier this year at a SGfuture dialogue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Fadli developed an interest in cybersecurity very early in his teens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He tried to enrol in an IT course at a polytechnic but was unsuccessful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Undeterred, he pursued private courses in IT and infocomm security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He worked various jobs to pay off his study loans and to gain experience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Eventually, he managed to graduate with a degree in cyber forensics, information security management and business information systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Today, he is Lead Intelligence Analyst at a cyber threat intelligence company.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Young Singaporeans like Fadli exemplify the spirit of SkillsFuture, and the new Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) will do all we can to help them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Cyber Security Agency (CSA) will also help to nurture Singaporeans' interest and awareness of cybersecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I will now	talk more about our cybersecurity efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Some hon Members have raised questions about cybersecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We established the CSA last year, as the national agency overseeing cybersecurity strategy, education and outreach and industry development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I am pleased to report that since its formation, we have made good progress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad asked how we can ensure executives of firms in critical sectors and important industries are committed to cyber security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: While bigger companies are better-equipped against cyber threats, cyber security is seldom a top priority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Businesses need to come around to the fact that cyber threats can hurt bottom lines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I am glad to share that CSA is working on an awareness programme to educate and sensitise the C-suite to potential cyber threats to their firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The hon Member also asked how cybersecurity awareness among individuals and businesses in Singapore is measured.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These figures are encouraging, but there is always room for improvement, especially as the threats grow more complex.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA advocates a multifaceted approach to cybersecurity, including risk-based mitigation, early detection and robust response.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Cross-sector responses are coordinated between CSA and other sectors to mitigate widespread cyberattacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ms Sun Xueling and Mr Vikram Nair asked about how CSA has worked with critical sectors to ensure resilience against cyberattacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA works closely with critical sectors to assess the critical infrastructure for vulnerabilities, taking a cybersecurity-by-design approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This ensures, Madam, that security capabilities and measures are in place to detect, respond to and recover from cyber threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To strengthen cyber resilience, CSA also conducts cybersecurity exercises with critical sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Recently, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean and I were present at CSA's multisector exercise, codenamed Exercise Cyber Star.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This exercise gave us the opportunity to evaluate the capabilities of CSA, the banking and finance, Government, energy and infocomm sectors in incident management as well as their operational processes and coordination functions in a simulated cyberattack.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I was pleased to observe that all parties worked well together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The exercise also saw a good demonstration of CSA's ability to mobilise resources and experts from across multiple sectors to address a crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: CSA will continue its close collaboration with various partners, including Government agencies, to better respond to cyberattacks and proceed with its plans to further build up its capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, as Members have pointed out, cyber threats are borderless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There are many international efforts that Singapore is involved in to strengthen cybersecurity cooperation, such as the ASEAN Computer Emergency Response Team Incident Drill and the ASEAN Regional Forum Seminar on operationalising cyber confidence-building measures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Last year, CSA also signed memoranda of understanding (MOUs) with the UK, France and India to strengthen international cyber security cooperation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Apart from building up the CSA's capabilities, we also intend to review the policy and legislative framework for cybersecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This is especially important as we move towards building Singapore as a Smart Nation and I thank the Members of the House who have asked about the proposed cybersecurity legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad and Mr Vikram Nair also asked how the legislation will complement the powers in the existing Computer Misuse and Cyber Security Act (CMCA).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, cyberattacks have increased in sophistication and attackers have become faster and bolder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It is inevitable that Singapore's critical information infrastructure will, at some point, be targets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The interconnectivity in our networks also means that the effects of cyberattacks can be contagious.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Globally, governments have been strengthening their cybersecurity legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In Germany, a law was passed last year to enforce minimum cybersecurity standards for critical infrastructure operators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It also mandates the reporting of significant cybersecurity incidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Last December, the US government approved the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, to facilitate the sharing of cyber threat information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The law also protects information sources from being sued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Broadly speaking, the Bill will ensure that operators take proactive steps to secure our critical information infrastructure and report incidents.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Many developed cities, such as New York, Seoul and Tokyo, are also investing in their public wi-fi infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Today's Wireless@SG speeds are slower in performance than what our 4G mobile networks provide.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Given our high penetration of smartphones among the population, this is also an opportunity to connect citizens with real-time data and sensor networks that will benefit them in areas such as transport and retail.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: An enhanced wireless infrastructure will also boost our workforce engaged in entrepreneurial or freelance opportunities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is the anticipated percentage of the rise in their bills after the withdrawal of this service?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister also explain how the Silver Infocomm Initiative has been rolled out and implemented to assist elderly Singaporeans who would be affected by this transition?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, are the outreach efforts available in Chinese dialects and the vernacular languages, such as Malay and Tamil, as well since our elderly comprise a very diverse group?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Despite medical advancements, the number of persons with functional disabilities, whether congenital or acquired, will increase.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore ramps up its drive to be a Smart Nation, it is critical that we integrate considerations of the needs of persons with functional disabilities in the planning process.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond infrastructural cost savings and business efficiency, Smart Nation can play a critical role in homecare and healthcare support and disability intervention and mitigation right from our homes, offices and community spaces, as well as mainstream integration of persons with functional disabilities and limitations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In this connection, can the Government give an update of the integration on such considerations?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: More than Smart Nation, let it be an instrument for One Nation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, you have three cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Having a pervasive public wi-fi network is becoming expected of smart cities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Many cities like Taipei, Helsinki and New York are investing heavily in free public wi-fi.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Link New York City (LinkNYC), an infrastructure project designed to create a network to cover NYC with free wi-fi service, was rolled out at the end of last year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It has been lauded for its gigabit speed Internet that will be available from 7,500 hotspots all over the city.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Singapore could do well to benefit from an extensive and high-quality wi-fi network in our push to become a smart nation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As wi-fi becomes increasingly important to tourists, public wi-fi capabilities would also be a point of attraction in our endeavours to boost our tourism sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Currently, Wireless@SG network is available for free until 31 March 2017.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How does the Government or MCI intend to enhance our Wireless@SG network?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Innovation and technology are increasingly crucial for productivity in all sectors and in enhancing the quality of life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We are now in the era that celebrates digital innovation and automated services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How does the Ministry intend to tap on this fund to develop Singapore's digital innovation capabilities in the Services and Digital Economy (SDE) domain?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Committee on the Future Economy was launched earlier this year, and corporate capabilities and innovation are among the key areas it will explore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Given that technology will undeniably be one of the key drivers of the future, how does the Ministry envision technology shaping Singapore's future economy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How will businesses be affected and how are they expected to adapt?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Many view these developments with anxiety: will a machine take over my work?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Will I be left behind as technology progresses?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We cannot pretend that as a small, open country, we can shield ourselves from these forces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The only way ahead is to prepare for the threats and opportunities and to try to be the disruptor rather than the disrupted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is what being a Smart Nation is about: we have a national plan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will develop, deploy and exploit digital technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will secure the future of our jobs and drive the transformation of our quality of life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will maintain the cohesiveness of our society, and our relevance to the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To succeed, everyone needs to come together: citizens, companies and the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What can the Government do to enable this vision of a Smart Nation?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Three things: first, we must build a first-class infrastructure for pervasive, seamless and high-speed connectivity to benefit citizens and businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Second, the Government must lead in the use of technology for our daily business: to serve people, make policy, plan ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In doing so, we will focus on public places, such as community clubs, hospitals, polyclinics, Government service centres, Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations, hawker centres, voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), retail and tourist spaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will increase the penetration and pervasiveness of Wireless@SG.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Already today, our hotspots-to-population ratio is second only to Tokyo.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our efforts and investments will help Singaporeans stay more connected.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to support this programme for as long as necessary because we need the wireless ecosystem to develop into one that is vibrant and self-sustaining.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is not the connectivity that makes us smart; it is what we do with it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need businesses to ride on our network to build and deploy new products and services, as alluded to by Assoc Prof Randolph Tan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are already new players in the market taking advantage of the open access mandate in broadband infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They provide a new range of products and services, such as real-time surveillance and time-critical financial data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Operators can also use Wireless@SG to offer improved services, such as cashless payment and location-based analytics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are forming the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) to drive transformation in the Government and to use digital technology to serve citizens better and improve our processes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One of the immediate responsibilities for GovTech is to roll out the Smart Nation Platform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Today, each Government agency collects their own data, deploys their own sensors and develops their own applications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Smart Nation Platform will provide a shared sensor communication platform for the whole-of-Government to allow collection, sharing and analysis of different types of data to benefit all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The first phase of Smart Nation Platform development and deployment is already under way, covering high traffic areas in the city and Yuhua.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The first priorities for using the data will be transport and security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Working with the Singapore Police Force (SPF) and the Land Transport Authority (LTA), we will be using the Smart Nation Platform video sensors and analytics to enable incident detection, vehicle count, speed analysis and crowd sensing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want to use the data to reduce crowdedness, improve bus waiting times and improve comfort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This citizen-centric impact is what we want to achieve, and the Smart Nation Platform is not just a bunch of devices but a way for different agencies to come together, and put citizens at the centre, build and share innovations that will serve people better.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is what GovTech is all about and I am confident that we can achieve this vision, with the support of all agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how we intend to develop Singapore's digital innovation capabilities under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2020.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is a collaboration among MCI, the Smart Nation Programme Office (SNPO) and the National Research Foundation (NRF) and will have two strategic imperatives: first, to support the development of digital technology in areas that affect citizens the most, such as transport, health and service productivity; and second, to build capabilities in platform technologies to open up possibilities for innovation in many different fields.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Examples are sensor communications, 3D geospatial science and cybersecurity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Globally, digital services were projected to have generated approximately US$1 trillion in revenues last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want Singapore business to share in this, to be part of this and to drive this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: With these investments and plans, we can make sure that we give our businesses every opportunity to be part of the global action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, leveraging on Singapore's access to Asian languages, Dr Li Haizhou from A*STAR's Institute for Infocomm Research is leading an international effort with over 27 countries to develop a multi-lingual speech translation service over the Internet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will enable 95% of the world's population to communicate with one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is an example of our competitive advantage as a result of the people that we have, the place that we occupy in the world, and the opportunities available to individuals, enterprises and academia here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The public sector can be the enabler and catalyst, but it is the private sector that needs to lead in innovation, to bring ideas from the research lab to the market, to deal with the disruption and be disruptors themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I am working together with representatives from the technology sector, such as Mr Caesar Sengupta, who is the Vice President of Google located here in Singapore, together with a group under the Committee on the Future Economy, to examine the impact of disruptive technologies on our economy and to come up with some recommendations for the Government, private enterprises and individual citizens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will look at how technology presents opportunities to re-engineer our business processes for better outcomes, leveraging on Singapore's competitive advantages, for example, our high level of connectivity, very high rate of literacy, as well as technological literacy and the high level of trust that exists in the Singapore brand name.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: At the same time, we must anticipate risks from new technologies, such as the threats to traditional businesses and jobs from automation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We must find ways to ease the transition for our people into new jobs and allow them to thrive in future work environments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have a vibrant startup ecosystem but, to seize the opportunities out there, this ecosystem needs to grow.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Last year, Infocomm Investments Pte Ltd (IIPL) set up a startup space called BASH, which stands for Build Amazing Startups Here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have found that our strategies also increase the survival rate of our startups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Lots of startup ideas exist and there is a lot of initial excitement, but a key part of the process is the ability of the startup to get past the initial stage and attract further follow-on funding and investment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Most have chosen to be based in Singapore, and, in turn, create jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This achievement would not be possible without a growing number of Singaporeans who are offering their time and expertise to help other aspiring entrepreneurs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He was the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of DS3, a Singapore-based company, before he moved on to Gemalto, a digital security MNC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He decided to make a mid-career change this year and became a full-time mentor at BASH.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: With his rich experience, he has been an extremely valuable resource for promising young entrepreneurs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He is advising several startups on issues like optimising shareholding, identifying good business channels and improving their business strategies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Thanks to such efforts, the quality of our startups is improving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More and more homegrown startups are developing products that could potentially transform their sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A graduate of IIPL's pre-acceleration programme, Jaga-Me is a local startup that connects patients and their families with quality home nursing services on-demand.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In doing so, it helps families to manage the stress of caregiving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The success of our Smart Nation will ultimately depend on the choices that we all make.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For BASH, their secret is experienced mentors like Teik Guan who wants to nurture the next batch of entrepreneurs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Government also needs people with the technical skills and the passion to serve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, IDA has launched the Smart Nation Fellowship Programme last month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This programme invites experienced Singaporean tech professionals to come into the Government and deliver meaningful digital and data solutions for citizens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: IDA has also pioneered a Technology Associates Programme to build a pipeline of technology leaders and experts for the Government through training and mentorship.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Over 350 applications were received for 15 spots under this programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Technology Associates have worked on projects such as the Business Grants portal announced by Minister Heng Swee Keat in the Budget and the online Student Learning Space being developed by the Ministry of Education (MOE).

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I am glad to see Singaporeans responding enthusiastically, not just to the Nerf Guns but also to our call to action to come and build our Smart Nation together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Even if you choose not to join the Government or work at BASH, there is a lot to do.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If you like to play with data or programme an app, visit our open data portal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We revamped it last year to make our data clearer and more meaningful.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is also machine-readable and, so, easier for anyone to use it to develop their own ideas and products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Here is a map from data.gov.sg that allows you to make a comparison among the telecom operators by region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If you click on the different hexagons or type in the address, you will be able to compare the speeds of the different operators at the places that you are interested in.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want to make data open, accessible and easy to use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want to encourage all the innovators out there to create something useful on top of our data, maximise its value for the public or do something just for the fun of it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is what the digital platform must do: bring us together as a people, each contributing our knowledge and experience in small and big ways and to be of service to one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is also why it is important that we take an inclusive approach as we take on the challenges and opportunities of the digital revolution and help one another adapt to the inevitable change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The bulk of them are not senior citizens, but rather foreigners living in Singapore, corporate users and prepaid users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: IDA is working with mobile operators to help them migrate smoothly to 3G and 4G networks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Other issues need more deliberate action, like bridging the digital divide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I attended a very nice multigenerational boot camp in Punggol East together with Mr Charles Chong and there were 10-year-old Primary 4 students training the people of their grandparents' age on how to access the various programmes on Toggle, how to do their online banking, and they were doing so in a mixture of English, Malay, Mandarin and Hokkien.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Today, Government websites are held to standards by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) for use by people with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But we are not satisfied to stop here and are looking at how e-Government services can be designed to better serve all Singaporeans, especially the elderly and people with special needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, the recent Budget 2016 speech had "live" captioning to enable the hearing-impaired and the deaf community to have direct access to the Budget speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong mentioned the Enabling Village.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This helps people with disabilities live and work independently using infocomm and assistive technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: She is 34 years old and born without limbs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Smart Nation is a rallying call to the Government, industry and all our citizens, and all of us need to work hand in hand and seize these possibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will need to take risks and be prepared for change and keep a look out for one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is about us and the relationships we build with one another, as one people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Ministry's support for public sector broadcasting has played an important role in keeping local content alive on television in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Now, the media landscape is set to change again; Netflix appears to be coming on the scene.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This is likely to provide even more competition to our local content.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Our local content has survived the challenge of cable TV; the question remains whether or not it is going to survive the challenge of Netflix.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I would be interested to know if the Ministry has any ideas on how we might help local PSB content remain relevant and interesting to Singaporeans to keep up with these new entrants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Besides the reviews to these channels, what improvements can be made to public service broadcasting (PSB) content on the vernacular channels?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Indeed, there is an increasing number of viewers who no longer even use an actual TV set to consume their content.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mobile phones, tablets, laptops, personal computer (PC) monitors, these are the screens that are becoming more popular.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: There are also new players entering the market, new genres of programmes and new production models as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Anyone who understands the references to "House of Cards" and "Orange is the New Black" will know what I am talking about.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Yet, in this landscape, I agree with my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Vikram Nair, that we cannot ignore the need for public service broadcasting (PSB).

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The programming for this dedicated free-to-air channel should be supported and managed by the respective stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The local theatre and performing arts scene could use a fully funded free-to-air arts channel to help artistes and performers promote their work and labour of love beyond the limited coverage given by the state-owned media.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The National Arts Council (NAC) said on its website that it celebrates excellence in the arts, and it will work to make it accessible to all.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: DVB-T2 will allow the vision to become a reality because everyone can have access to free-to-air channels using the mobile device in his or her hand.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The sports scene in our school will certainly breathe a new lease of life and excitement if such competitive events are covered and broadcast on free-to-air PSB channels.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Such programmes can be produced and directed by the many arts and communications students in our polytechnics and universities as part of their curriculum and training.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I believe our students would love to take on the challenge to produce such programmes and have their production carried on free-to-air channels.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The experience these students acquire in the course of doing that is immeasurable.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The arrival of digital broadcasting in Singapore presents a wonderful opportunity for regulators and policymakers to deepen the skillsets of our own talents and broaden the scope of our expertise to become a media hub in the region.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It also presents an opportunity for regulators to widen the PSB Framework to include areas which were not given much attention in the past.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Today, our media content producers and broadcasters, predominantly Mediacorp and StarHub, provide public service broadcasting to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Can the Ministry elaborate on its plans to ensure that the public service broadcast (PSB) will continue to reach out to Singaporeans in this new digital landscape?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As our public service broadcasters face greater competition, what are the Ministry's strategies to ensure that they remain competitive and continue to provide local content to compete more effectively against more sophisticated media players that have global reach and economies of scale?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Is the Ministry considering adding more local players such as Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) or SingTel, or others who meet the requirements, to further develop the PSB options for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: What are the Ministry's plans to enhance the use of social and digital media as channels for PSB?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Today, our public service broadcasters also provide avenues for developing local talent.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: PSB providers, therefore, become a platform to grow local talent, strengthen our production capabilities and, hopefully, some may become world beaters.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, I hope that through PSB, the Government will also place a strong emphasis on investing in our local talent pool and ensure that the sector continues to provide good jobs and opportunities for all.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I declare my interest as a co-founder of a media production agency.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I never thought much about Public Service Broadcasting (PSB) until I thought about how we can use it to help disrupt the poverty cycle here.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In the 1980s, two psychologists investigated why Head Start, America's programme for uplifting poor children, was having limited success.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And the gap is not just in number, but tone, complexity and type of words as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not have the Singapore statistics, but I am betting we will see similar patterns.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Research shows that many children in our poorest households stay at home because going out costs their parents too much money and inconvenience.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: These kids attend preschool inconsistently and cannot go for enrichment classes like their richer peers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, they spend their time watching Youtube and TV at home.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our PSB funding can be so much more deliberate in what social good it can achieve.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Growing income and educational inequality is a real problem here.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
