text: What if we carved out some of our PSB funds to create programmes for TV and Youtube that focused on closing this 32-million word gap?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Could the funds encourage producers to collaborate with educators and researchers to deliver innovative children's programmes guided by educational curriculum?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What if we also asked for a cast that reflected racial and socioeconomic diversity and a show that promotes empathy and even very basic bilingualism?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If you think that sounds way too idealistic or boring, it has actually been done before to tremendous effect.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It was the first time a children's TV show was not just co-created with educators, but simultaneously monitored by researchers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Its producers developed the Children's Television Workshop (CTW) model, a system of TV show planning, production and evaluation based on collaborations among producers, writers, educators, and researchers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The world has not seen another Sesame Street.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But maybe now is the time for one to rise in Asia, and I think Singapore is a perfect place to give it a go.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Let it be a gift, not just for the poor in our own country, but to Asia and the world.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Public expectations of Government communications have heightened, with increased scrutiny on how the Government postures and positions policies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In our diverse society, the Government needs to customise its approach in communicating policies and handling crises, especially to its intended target segments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There are many schemes covered in this Budget, and how each citizen will benefit from it will vary.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: How can the Government leverage its experience with the Pioneer Generation Package and extend it to simplify the communications on more complex policies such as MediShield Life, CPF LIFE and the many different housing schemes being rolled out?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must make simplifying our complex policies a habit in our communications, so that the ordinary citizen can easily "get it" and be clear on the benefits, rationale and trade-offs in each of our policies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Commercial service providers today and also applications are increasingly moving towards personalisation, targeted outreach and being able to push recommendations in how their products are being marketed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Will the Government go the same way to reach each Singaporean in his or her mode of communications, be it email, short message service (SMS), mailers, booths or even adverts on the street?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ultimately, can the Ministry share how it plans to further strengthen public communications to reach different groups of Singaporeans more effectively?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The old channels of television, radio and newspapers face unprecedented competition and are struggling to maintain their audience.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This proliferation of media has made Government communications more and more challenging.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Whereas in the past, there were only a few channels that were consumed by the vast majority, we now instead have an intricate tapestry of different media, each targeting a different audience.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, the audience has become more and more discerning and demanding.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: No longer forced to accept whatever was delivered to them, they now pick and choose what they watch or listen to.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our diverse society, it is clear that a one-size-fits-all approach to communications no longer works.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A successful communications strategy must tailor both message and medium for the intended audience.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This cleverly use different forms of communications that were designed to gain the attention of the elderly, for example, by using Teochew opera.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Ministry share how it plans to further strengthen public communications to reach different groups of Singaporeans more effectively?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Combined with an ageing population, the need for quality translations is more crucial than ever.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the work of the National Translation Committee (NTC) to meet this need in the long term?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, the Tamil community is one of the smallest and we often get feedback on issues with Tamil translations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I suspect this also has to do with resource constraints.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Are there any plans to improve the quality of Tamil translations services?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Quality design can also be a strategic tool to help firms to expand their businesses globally and develop a Singapore brand.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our city, town and community planning have won many accolades.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the years, we have planned and developed Singapore into a liveable and lovable city where our people enjoy a good quality of life.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Two, what is the role of design in fulfilling the aspirations of Singapore to be a Smart Nation?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Today, more and more businesses, even in traditionally non-design fields, are utilising design strategies and design thinking toolkits in planning better customer experiences and product innovations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: My own experience as an educator and part of the team at the School of Design in Temasek Polytechnic has reinforced how critical it is to embed design awareness and appreciation into young people as a whole.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: While this is commendable and desirable, I hope that the Ministry could share their plans on how they intend to move this forward.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Given the already highly packed school curriculum geared towards high-stakes exams, design studies and design appreciation should not be tagged on as an afterthought, or be perceived as an unnecessary addition to the already heavy load our young students bear.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: In fact, I believe it should be integrated as seamlessly as possible, through lively discussions and exposure to arts, popular culture, photography, film, fashion, architecture and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The dialogue with design begins at the primary school level at least and should continue into the later years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I believe this is important as this exposure to design and design thinking should be for all students and not just for those who want to pursue a career in the creative industries.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Having such an early foundation produces curious and innovative thinkers who are analytical, bold, experimental and expressive, skillsets that would serve them well in this 21st century world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This would perhaps lead to the creativity and innovation of our society that my Parliamentary colleague, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, was talking about in her earlier Budget debate speech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: There should not be a one-size-fits-all approach to design education and greater autonomy should be given to design schools to shape their own pedagogy, for example, the formation of smaller class sizes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I know we talked about class sizes in the COS debate when the Minister for Education spoke.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I do not want to go into this now, but suffice to say that, coming from the ground, it does make a difference when you teach subjects like design to have smaller class sizes – admission based more on aptitude, passion and interest than aggregate at the various entry points; and the recruitment of design lecturers from the pool of design practitioners based on skill sets and experience, rather than educational and academic qualifications.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I sincerely hope that MCI will engage MOE and various other stakeholders in a deeper discussion to make all these aspects of design education realistically possible.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The next area to consider, then, is accreditation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: With the many design courses in the market and so many education providers, professional accreditation and benchmarking are important to maintain standards in the industry.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Copious amounts of research have shown that reading is critical to children's neural, intellectual and even socio-cultural development.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Reading also introduces children to magical worlds of adventure and fantasy that allows them to develop creatively.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I would just like to ask the Ministry if we can do more to nurture a love for reading, not just among the young in our schools, but also for young adults, adults and even seniors, and possibly across different languages as well.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In fact, tiny bursts of information in the form of short Facebook posts, Instagram pictures and Twitter, have dominated the communication of ideas, and reading a book almost seems to run counter to the trend in the age of instantaneous gratification and information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But reading has a part to play in our drive for creativity and innovation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In the bestseller "Natural History of Innovation", the author, Steven Johnson, discusses the role serendipity plays in innovation and identifies reading as one of the best ways to cultivate serendipity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He suggests that the accidental combination of ideas that powers serendipity requires an abundance of ideas and for them to reside in one's memory waiting for an instance to associate with one another.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Reading plays a key role in transmitting ideas to the reader and, where there is opportunity to read a variety of books over a compressed period of time, creates possibilities of serendipitous collisions among the ideas of different book authors.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is interesting that the founder of Facebook and promoter of bite-sized information bits, Mark Zuckerberg, has set up a Facebook book club and, to quote him: "My challenge for 2015 is to read a new book every other week, with an emphasis on learning about different cultures, beliefs, histories and technologies".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Given the importance of reading, can we kick-start a reading movement and have role models share the impact that reading has on their lives?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Further, young residents would greatly benefit from earlier access to libraries.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: One can only truly value how far we have come by understanding where we came from and how we did so.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: At the same time, the rapid changes in Singapore's urban landscape can create the impression that everything is new and temporary and that our heritage has been sacrificed in the name of progress.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: How are we riding the wave of increased interest in Singapore's history brought about by the SG50 celebrations?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: I am sure the National Library Board (NLB) can accomplish much more with the help of the community.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: How could we build upon this momentum and encourage more Singaporeans to contribute and enrich NLB's collections of our history and heritage?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: In this digital age, the preservation of our heritage, be it pictures, videos, oral recordings or text, becomes easier, but also, in some ways, less tangible.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Since there often is no physical object that the user can interact with in a tactile way, we need to combine technology with physical records, and this suggests a role for libraries and archives.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: What plans does the Ministry have for libraries and archives in nation-building?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: The other challenge for nation-building efforts is the need to compete with all the other sources of information and entertainment out there.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Most Singaporeans probably know more about other countries from watching travel documentaries than they do about the rich history of their home.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: For example, most Singaporeans are quite unaware that the National Archives holds a rich historical collection.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: We should help them discover this hidden treasure and enrich their understanding of the Singapore story.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: How would the National Archives improve public access to its heritage materials?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will speak about MCI's priorities in three areas: strengthening Public Service Broadcasting (PSB), enhancing Government communications and translation, and expanding the role of design in our lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PSB is an important part of our lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PSB programmes not only entertain and educate Singaporeans, they also reflect our societal values, celebrate our local heritage and help shape the Singapore identity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: News and current affairs programmes keep Singaporeans well-informed about the world around us and unite Singaporeans with shared experiences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For instance, we mourned as one during the National Mourning week last year when our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew passed away.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we cheered with one heart during our SG50 National Day Parade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Only locally produced PSB programmes can have such effects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Foreign programmes will not reflect our local values and culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through PSB programmes, our media industry players can tell the Singapore story from a Singaporean perspective and with a Singaporean heart.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That is why the Government has long supported PSB and, indeed, increased our funding for PSB in recent years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Like many other countries – Britain with the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), Japan with the Nippon Hōsō Kyōkai (NHK) – we recognise the importance of PSB.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Mr Ganesh Rajaram observed, this sustained investment has enabled Singaporeans to enjoy many more quality programmes over free-to-air TV and radio, as well as through online platforms like Toggle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Channel 8's "118", which addresses social topics in a light-hearted way, reaches more than one million viewers every week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Channel 5's "Tanglin" is watched by more than 300,000 viewers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Suria and Vasantham have grown their viewership significantly in the last few years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I visited them recently and was impressed by how they have built strong relationships with their audiences, organising community roadshows so that the public can meet the stars in person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Darryl David asked if PSB funds support media organisations other than Mediacorp.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Since 2013, we have also set aside some PSB funding for independent producers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For instance, this has enabled companies, like WaWa Pictures, to produce shows like Crescendo, or 起飞.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The show included a live xinyao concert for the public that was featured in the series' finale.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through this show, Singaporeans learnt about the development of xinyao and the Chinese music scene here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am encouraged by the progress that Mediacorp and our media companies have made.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But the operating environment for our media companies is getting more challenging.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our viewers are consuming content from a variety of sources such as Netflix, iTunes, Spotify and many others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Free-to-air TV has to jostle to keep the attention of viewers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have spoken about how additional investments in PSB have improved the quality of PSB content.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will not be able to match the budgets of blockbuster American productions like Game of Thrones, or Korean drama Descendants of the Sun.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we can find other innovative ways to attract viewers by producing quality local content by focusing on our cultural heritage and featuring interesting aspects of Singapore society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have had several of such well-received programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mediacorp dramas like "The Little Nyonya" in the past and, more recently, excellent documentaries commissioned by Mediacorp like "Wild City – Islands" and "All Access Changi".

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These were produced by Beach House Pictures, an independent production company founded by Mr Donovan Chan and Ms Jocelyn Little in 2005.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This brings me to my second point – building strong capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PSB funding plays a useful role to support Mediacorp and local media companies to attract, train and retain their Singaporean talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides funding, we want to create opportunities for learning and collaboration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In May last year, we launched Fox Format Labs, a partnership between MDA and Fox International channels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Fox worked with five Singapore production companies to produce content for National Geographic Channel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through the collaboration, our companies could screen their shows to an international audience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am pleased that the industry has responded positively to our initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr William Lim from Xtreme Media said this was "exactly what local producers need".

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must also continue to raise our capabilities in storytelling, set design and videography.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When I visited the set of "Tanglin"¸ I met its group of talented scriptwriters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They work in a team, constantly learning from one another and also challenging one another to think of fresh ideas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mediacorp also brought in Ms Kathleen Beedles as a consultant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She is a UK producer who has worked on several successful dramas like the long-running Emmerdale, which has been on the air in the UK since 1972.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Working with somebody like Ms Beedles gave our local production team and our young talents opportunities to learn from experts in their field.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, we must proactively embrace new channels to reach audiences who are consuming news and entertainment through different media.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many Singaporeans today, especially the young, spend a lot of time online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, PSB must extend its reach online to engage and connect with our audiences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The increase in viewership was especially significant after its relaunch in April 2015.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I met the Toggle team during my visit to Mediacorp and congratulated them on their success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I also urged them to continue to look for innovative ways to increase Toggle's reach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Toggle is a great platform to experiment with new concepts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The first, "A Selfie's Tale" by Oak3 Films, has done well so far with 600,000 views.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PSB funds have also supported "Pursuit of Champions", a documentary about young Singaporean athletes, produced by The Moving Visuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This programme is currently available on StarHub Go.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore Airlines also acquired the programme for its inflight entertainment, bringing local content to an international audience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must ensure that our channels remain relevant and can meet viewers' preferences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked about Mediacorp's review of Okto and Channel U.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mediacorp is exploring the idea of positioning Okto as a channel focusing on children and young adults, as well as sports.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have been discussing with Mediacorp on the idea of including coverage for school sports.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think there is value to supporting quality PSB programmes for children, as Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin has suggested.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have a good local children's programme called "Mat Yoyo".

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As for Channel U, Mediacorp is examining ways to further enhance its Chinese content, which is currently delivered through Channel 8 and Channel U.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the years, our vernacular channels have contributed significantly to the development of bilingualism here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They allow Singaporeans to stay connected to our language, culture and communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides Chinese programming, we will also ensure that Suria and Vasantham have adequate resources to continue producing quality programmes to serve our different ethnic communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The successful transformation of PSB will require persistence and hard work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our industry players like Mediacorp need to have a steadiness to ride through business cycles, and not allow short-term commercial ups and downs to affect the longer-term goals of producing good quality content, building strong capabilities and developing effective channels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Public broadcasters in many countries face difficulties due to increased competition from online media and falling advertising revenue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It moved its youth-focused TV channel, BBC Three, entirely online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also plans to overhaul its organisational structure in response to these challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government is fully supportive of this review and we will work closely with Mediacorp and Temasek Holdings in this effort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We want to help Mediacorp to further strengthen the three "C"s – content, capabilities and channels – so that the company can continue to do well as Singapore's national broadcaster and produce good quality local programmes for Singaporeans to enjoy for years to come.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad and Mr Ong Teng Koon asked about further strengthening Government communications for different groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We believe communications is an integral part of policy formulation and implementation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have built up stronger communication capabilities over the past few years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Looking ahead, we will continue to focus on three areas: content, platforms and languages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, we need to create engaging content that can connect with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The most powerful and effective messages are simple to understand and contain a strong emotional element that people can relate to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MCI worked with Mr Jeff Cheong and his team from Tribal to pilot a new approach for our recent MediShield Life video, "Love of a Lifetime".

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It had one simple message – just as the love between a husband and wife is lifelong, so, too, is the lifelong coverage of MediShield Life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, MCI will use multiple platforms and channels to reach different segments of the population.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, we revamped Gov.sg and optimised it for mobile devices because that is what more people are using these days.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are now looking at Instagram and Telegram to supplement our communications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At the same time, we recognise that online platforms are not for everyone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Face-to-face interactions will continue to be a key part of Government communications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A good example is how Pioneer Generation (PG) Ambassadors communicate with the elderly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2015, awareness of the PG Package among Pioneers reached 96%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We want to help our seniors to understand how they can benefit from different Government policies and measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We can build on the PG Ambassadors network and expand it to reach more seniors beyond Pioneers and to explain a range of Government policies beyond the Pioneer Generation Package and MediShield Life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Mr Ong Teng Koon that this is important to strengthen Government communication in Chinese, Malay and Tamil.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, we started the Information Service (Translation) Scholarship to groom more translation talents for the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is important to nurture passion from young and help our students to see the relevance of translation in their daily lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will work with schools and community partners to reach out to more young Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):   Early this year, we launched the Community in Translation initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through this platform, we hope to plan and organise various activities together with the community to raise awareness and interest in translation among our young.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our ultimate goal is to groom more translation talents and raise our translation standards in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This February, we held an English-to-Chinese translation workshop with the Ministry of Education (MOE).

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More than 80% of the participants found the workshop useful, informative and fun.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They felt that they acquired useful knowledge related to translation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are delighted to know that some students indicated that they would continue to learn translation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also plan to hold similar workshops and other translation-related activities in Malay and Tamil later this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This event is currently ongoing and will conclude in April.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As with the translation workshop, we are looking to expand this to Malay and Tamil and use creative methods to increase the interest in translation among our young.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In English): Mr Vikram Nair asked what we can do to improve Tamil translations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Indeed, this topic was raised at a recent NTC meeting, as we had observed a number of Tamil translation errors in recent months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These were avoidable errors, and they should not have been made in the first place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have reminded all Government agencies that it is important to get their translations done properly, including Tamil translations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have also asked NTC and its Tamil Resource Panel to conduct a systemic review and recommend areas for improvement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The review will be led by Parliament Interpreter Mr A Palaniappan, who is heading the Tamil Resource Panel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will also involve other community leaders with expertise and passion in Tamil language and translation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To our friends from the Tamil community, I would like to say: (In Tamil) Correct translation is our commitment!

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (சரியான மொழிபெயர்ப்பே, நமது கடப்பாடு!) (In English): We are committed to doing better and getting our translations done correctly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin and Mr Darryl David asked about the Design 2025 Masterplan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through the Masterplan, we want to support them further, so that they can grow and thrive beyond our shores.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: About 80% of firms have at least one accredited Landscape Architect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Among them is Mr Franklin Po of Tierra Design, winner of the President's Design Award in 2015.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Franklin is a Singaporean designer who used to work in the US before he returned to start Tierra Design.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also plan to expand the programme to include other design sectors, starting with interior designers, and urban designers and planners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another initiative is the Singapore Good Design Mark (SG Mark).

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This recognises exceptionally designed products and services that are developed in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the last three years, SG Mark has gained considerable traction with our trade partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will work with the Design Business Chamber of Singapore to further establish SG Mark as a regional standard for good design.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a major consumer of design services, the Government, too, can play a part by providing opportunities to design firms of all sizes to take part in Government projects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This way, promising local firms will get the chance to demonstrate their capabilities and build up their track records.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When I met some of the local designers, they told me that such opportunities are more important and more valuable for them than Government grants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also want to involve our citizens and communities in the design process to co-create conducive spaces to live, work and play.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In Yuhua, for example, the DesignSingapore Council is working with the Citizens' Consultative Committee to organise co-creation sessions for residents and community leaders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During these sessions, participants get to redesign and co-create programmes to engage their communities and enhance the experiences of residents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This user-centric approach is key not only in design, but also in our journey towards a Smart Nation, as noted by Dr Teo Ho Pin.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Design humanises technology and makes it smarter and more user-friendly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Darryl David mentioned that design is not only for designers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is something that can benefit everyone and across different sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To achieve these goals, the Government needs to work closely with our industry and community partners, so that together, we can create a better future for ourselves, our children and generations to come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I would now like to talk about our efforts to further inculcate the habit of reading and its impact on how we will continue developing and growing as a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We can read to learn, to broaden our minds and perspectives of the world around us, or simply for leisure and enjoyment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It can also be a means to open new doors and opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Last month, I attended an NLB SGFuture engagement session at the library@orchard and spoke with many participants there about reading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: They shared very passionately about why they thought reading is important and how we can encourage more to read.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: One of the young adults at the session, in particular, had this to say, and I quote: "I grew up very poor and books were my only escape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: When I was a child, my mother and father split and they both remarried, and somehow the first ‘set' of children got lost in that whole mess… But in books you find an escape without going very far.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The people I met at SGFuture make me believe that NLB can do even more, by making reading convenient, enjoyable and interesting for everyone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This is why we will begin the next lap of our journey as a society by redoubling our awareness and emphasis on reading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To meet these objectives, NLB will focus on three priorities for the Reading Movement as a start.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Darryl David asked about how we could promote reading not just among the young but to all members of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Indeed, Madam, we have done very well in helping children read, through our kidsRead and Read@School programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will now turn our attention to services for adults.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: While many adults visit our libraries, we often see them borrowing books for their children, more so than for themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: So, we want to help adults rediscover the joy of reading for themselves so as to be a role model for their children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Hence, to make it easy and convenient for us to find interesting reads, NLB will bring books to people, instead of merely encouraging people to come to the books.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will bring good content and services to working adults in the office and when they are on the move.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will do this by curating and pushing out short reads and articles to commuters, which they can read on their mobile devices during a train ride or while waiting at the bus stop.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Anyone with a mobile device can scan a QR code to download recommended e-books via the NLB mobile app or access other content like short essays during their train journey.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: NLB will also run a Spot-A-Reader campaign on social media to recognise and encourage readers on board this train.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, NLB will curate reads on common management topics, industry trends that are useful for work or even a good piece of short fiction for leisure reading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Some partners which NLB has already started working with are DBS and the National Trades Union Congress’ U Associate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Through reading, they will be able to keep their minds healthy and alert, as they stay abreast of current affairs and learn new things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Therefore, NLB will expand the range of reading programmes that cater to the many interests and needs of our seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These programmes include do-it-yourself craft groups and also writing workshops where seniors can discuss autobiographies and perhaps even pen down their own memoirs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will also bring books to the elderly if they are unable to visit the library.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Earlier this month, I visited the Thye Hwa Kwan Senior Services Centre at Taman Jurong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The centre has over 1,000 members and was the first Senior Activity Centre to partner NLB in 2012.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Today, it runs programmes to promote reading and learning among the elderly through hands-on activities like origami workshops.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It also has a reading corner set up by NLB with fiction and non-fiction books that are refreshed on a quarterly basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: If there is interest among residents to set up and lead in running an "interim" library in a new estate without an existing library, NLB will facilitate residents' efforts in doing so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We can provide a seed collection and equip volunteers with sufficient know-how to run this interim library independently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As Ms Sun has pointed out, this is already being done in Sengkang, where volunteers have set up a community library in a container with books from NLB because the Sengkang Public Library is temporarily closed due to renovations at Compass Point.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: By being innovative about how we approach the reading endeavour, and by focusing our attention on adults and seniors, we hope to make reading a convenient, relevant and accessible part of everyone's lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Reading is a gateway to culture and reading in one's mother tongue cultivates an understanding of languages, culture and history.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Reading widely in more than one language also helps build a strong foundation for bilingual literacy in our children, as stories are a fun way to ignite children's love for the language.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: NLB has encouraged reading in Chinese, Malay and Tamil in many different ways – through exhibitions, publications, book displays, reading clubs for adults and children and week-long Mother Tongue Language Festivals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These, Madam, have been very well-received by the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These reading clubs have ignited interest in reading and helped to improve participants' language skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: One such participant is eight-year-old Dhiya Durrani Ashraf Adri, a Primary 2 student from Junyuan Primary who is a regular at the club Kelab Wira Pintar, or the Smart Heroes Reading Club, at the Tampines Regional Library.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: His mother noticed that, since his participation in this club, Dhiya's Malay vocabulary has improved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The first project is a news and current affairs interest group led by Zaobao and Wanbao journalists at the Toa Payoh Public Library.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This group, which just started in March, will meet regularly at the library to discuss news articles and issues of the day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: NLB is also working with other media organisations to promote reading in other mother tongue languages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Apart from newspapers and books at our public libraries, our National Library also puts on exhibitions of very intriguing multilingual books from their collections.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Among the items displayed in the ongoing exhibition "From the Stacks" are early dictionaries, like the Hokkien-Malay dictionary which was published in the 1880s and used by the Hokkien-speaking Chinese population to help them in their conversations with their Malay neighbours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This dictionary transposes the phonetic sounds of Malay words into Chinese characters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, the Chinese character for "9" or 九 is presented with three other accompanying Chinese characters below it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These characters, when read in Hokkien, sound like "sem-bi-lan", the Malay word for "9".

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Books like this not only give us a glimpse of the context and culture of their time, but also show us how important such bilingual books are in bridging the natural language divides of the various races in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This then leads to a deeper understanding of one another's culture, resulting in stronger community ties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To create a vibrant reading culture, NLB will work with partners from all sectors – individuals, businesses, Government agencies and others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In fact, the NTUC, Zaobao, Wanbao and LTA partnerships that I mentioned earlier are but the start of many more collaborations that NLB is embarking on to encourage reading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Organisations and educational institutions will also be invited to take part in the pledging to get their staff and students to read.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I hope Singapore Parliament will join soon, Madam.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The pledging campaign will end with an inaugural National Reading Day on 30 July.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: On that day, we hope to see everyone reading, be it in groups or otherwise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We hope to focus the nation's attention on reading and to encourage busy Singaporeans to set aside time to read by creating opportunities for people to Read Together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The National Reading Day will, of course, be organised with the help of the community, public and private sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: By reaching out to new audience segments, putting a renewed focus on reading in mother tongue, and expanding our partnerships and networks, we hope to galvanise all Singaporeans into adopting reading as a lifestyle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To ascertain how best they can play this role, NLB will be conducting a nationwide survey on Singaporeans' reading habits this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The insights gathered will help us to finetune our long-term plans for how the library can help promote reading and learning, be it through the National Reading Movement, physical libraries or other library resources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: While we put all these initiatives in place, we must also remember that reading goes far beyond what the libraries can do; it extends to each and every one of us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The SGFuture sessions that NLB has organised so far – one in English and the other in Mandarin – have given us many good ideas on how to encourage more to read, such as books-on-the-go, "gamifying" reading, and having Reading Ambassadors for mother tongue languages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Some of these ideas are already being taken up by NLB.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will have another two SGFuture sessions coming up soon, in Malay and Tamil, and I look forward to hearing even more ideas from the public so that we can co-create solutions together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It is only with the community's help that the Reading Movement can be a truly national one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I agree with him that there is great potential for the community to play an active part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Since 2011, the "Singapore Memory Project" has been a good platform for Singaporeans to share their memories and stories of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This has helped in understanding who we are and where we came from, and this will help to strengthen our national identity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Our historical records are enriched by these contributors offering both their time and knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In the ensuing years, we will continue to enhance outreach efforts, introduce more programmes, provide greater access to archival records and encourage more Singaporeans to partner us in uncovering our history.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will also improve physical access through revamps of our gallery spaces so that our heritage and past can resonate even better with Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The push to become Smart, that is, connected, knowledgeable and engaged, is a global endeavour that our country is very much a part of.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Everything that my Ministry has set out to do is about connecting Singaporeans with the community, the Government and opportunity, with the help of trustworthy infrastructure and cutting-edge technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To be ready for the future also means being innovative and enterprising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: So, we will invest in research and launch programmes which will apply emerging technologies to improve productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: At the same time, we will build up the Government's design and engineering capabilities so as to provide better digital Government services for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ultimately, our singular aim is to improve the quality of life for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I hope the initiatives that we have shared today will lay the groundwork for Singapore to thrive in our next lap of development and maturity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My question is directed to the Minister of State on the cessation of 2G services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: How many elderly Singaporeans are affected by the cessation of these services and how many of them are on prepaid plans?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Would the Ministry consider a voucher or rebate scheme in conjunction with the telecommunications companies to assist these elderly Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I do not have the exact number of the prepaid as opposed to post-paid plans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The overall number is likely to be low.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it is actually hard to be sure when the registrant is not always the user.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The migration from 2G to 3G is necessary because the 2G radio spectrum is to be freed up for many of our ongoing plans for improving connectivity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do want to find a way to ensure that these elderly stay in touch.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is an important part of the connectivity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I need to go and look into this specific question that the Member has brought up and I will do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Whether a rebate scheme is necessary, my understanding is that their current 2G subscription plans will continue even if the device has to be changed to a 3G device in order for them to access this spectrum.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the intent we all have is the same as what the Member has raised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do want to ensure that the elderly who are currently using mobile devices will have every opportunity to continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram
text: With regard to PSB content, with 40% being actually farmed out by Mediacorp to independent production companies, would the Ministry think about actually making the contract as well as the projects and the amounts public so that there is more transparency between the independent production community and the platforms?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram
text: The second question is: given what is happening in Iskandar and the rise of Pinewood Studios, how are we trying to encourage companies within the Mediapolis to step up and fare better with the competition?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the first question, indeed, a significant proportion, up to 40% of PSB through Mediacorp, can be outsourced and Mediacorp has been doing that to support local media companies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The process in which they do that is that they would call for proposals and, in addition to what Mediacorp does, we also have a contestable funding that we do, separate of Mediacorp, that could go to a range of different companies as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, strengthening of PSB, it is important, and we do look for different opportunities, whether through Mediacorp, that means produced in-house by Mediacorp, or through Mediacorp to outsource to independent producers, or directly from the contestable funds to support independent producers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As to Mr Rajaram's second question on Iskandar, I think that is why we cannot stand still in this industry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is fast-moving, and convergence is one challenge.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I see it also as an opportunity for some breakthrough and innovation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is both a challenge as well as an opportunity for breakthrough.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What we need in the end, because it is such a talent-driven industry, is that building capabilities would be a very key part of any strategy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Whether there is Iskandar or not, I think we do need to build up capabilities, strengthen the production of local content, strengthen capabilities and develop effective channels because the competition is not just physically next door.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It can come from as far as from Northeast Asia, across the Pacific from America.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because in today's day and age, the competition can come from anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: He talked about the effectiveness of the outreach for PG.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: I want to ask if the use of dialects in those promotional videos is a contributing factor, as well as what is the Ministry's stand on the use of dialects in our broadcast in view of reaching out to the elderly in a more effective and engaging manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This has been used as part of the overall communication strategy in addition to the broadcast media, in addition to, very importantly, face-to-face interaction between our PG Ambassadors and the Pioneers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is what we want to try and do, which is to use a range of different channels and platforms and to customise the messages in a way which is simple to understand, is able to connect and use these platforms and these effective communication messages to reach out to different target audiences, whether it is the elderly, working adults, or the young.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is something which I covered in my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We want to enhance the content, make it engaging, look for different platforms and use different languages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I have a question for the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In my speech earlier, I spoke about the possibility of expanding PSB to include other new players.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I want to ask whether the Ministry is considering that or is in dialogue with any new players and whether it is considering bringing in new players.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Would independent broadcasters or providers also be included if they meet certain requirements?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Next, I noticed that when it comes to Government public communications, the translation for materials and publicity for the Malay and Tamil languages always come later.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I would assume that in doing translation, there would be separate teams and probably with different capacities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, do we have a capacity issue that some of these translations for the Malay and Tamil language materials come much later and whether the Government has sufficient talent and resources to upkeep the standards of Malay and Tamil translations for Government materials?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And we want to do this because, in the end, it is about being able to produce good quality Singapore content, tell the Singapore story and engage our audiences.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This can be done by Mediacorp but it can also be done by other players, whether it is directly through contestable funding or through Mediacorp.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: One important point I want to stress is this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mediacorp plays a very critical role as our national broadcaster.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: While we want to support the independent producers and grow many of these local media companies, create good jobs for Singaporeans, it is also important that while we do that, we must provide the necessary support and resources to help Mediacorp to succeed because, as a national broadcaster, there are certain important roles that they play to shape the Singapore identity, spread Singapore values, heritage and culture.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We should work not as a zero-sum game but on how we can strengthen Mediacorp and the local media industry together.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As to Mr Zaqy Mohamad's second point about translation, this is a challenge for all languages.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And, in fact, our friends from the media will sometimes tell us that when we send out information, it is very often done in English and, for the Chinese papers, the Malay papers, the Tamil papers, they have to spend quite a lot of time to do the translation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is difficult for us to have large numbers but we do not need large numbers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I am confident that with the support of our community, media friends, resource panels and language experts, we can do it.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I applaud what Minister of State Janil Puthucheary shared, regarding the promotion of ICT startups.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Smart Nation serves as the lead user of technology and creates demand for local solutions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But for a startup to scale up, they need to solve big problems such as those of international markets.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: How is MCI supporting our ICT startups to internationalise and provide solutions for international markets?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Given that company-led training is, perhaps, the most direct way to ensure skills fit to jobs, how do we encourage more companies to provide on-the-job training?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, it is an important part of how a start-up has to deal with the brutal realities of both the technological space as well as our small market.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Very early on in the development of a technologically based start-up, they do need to consider an internationalisation strategy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The mentors that we are bringing in through IIPL and BASH and several other mechanisms, a guide is that enthusiastic young people driving the startups have to think about internationalisation strategies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The young people themselves need to have some opportunity to expose themselves to what happens outside of our own market.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That means that the companies that are operating either in the region or internationally need to be located here to provide these opportunities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, there are multiple things that we need to do.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it comes down to connecting the businesses here with opportunities in the region, connecting the people here with businesses that operate outside of Singapore and educating them as they develop their business, as they develop their startups think about the internationalisation strategy very, very early on in the process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are a number of things that we need to do at MCI, and its partners are very much focused on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We manage to get a few companies to come and be involved in the Tech Skills Accelerator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The programmes below this can be part of it, but the Tech Skills Accelerator will also define new skill sets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I think we need to go out and reach out to the companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Therefore, it is a very, very good programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I agree with the Member that this is something which we should encourage more companies to do and IDA will continue to get more companies on board.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Apart from written translation, you and I know that if we have a programme which is a video, for example, PG in Mandarin or in English, to translate that into Malay you cannot do a direct translation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Obviously, the nuances are different, the cultural backgrounds are different and, therefore, you need talent, you need companies that can do that within the cultural context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Currently, there may not be many companies which are able to do so but our staff have been working very hard to be able to roll out the PG Package in different languages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It shows that we can do it with a lot of effort where we built a lot of capability, and we hope we can also energise the private sector to step forward and think about what they can do to help us in the upcoming Government communications of the new policies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is always a perception that the application of technologies is for the young and the savvy.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, it is great to know that many applications being piloted under Smart Nation, are also for the elderly and seniors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In terms of deployment of assistive technologies and how we can make applications more inclusive for seniors, what are IDA's plans to make this so?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is, again, something that is not based on a single strategy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are a number of things that we have to think about.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It comes in right at the beginning of the design stage, whatever the strategy or whatever the platform, whatever the issue to bring in that thinking about making sure that people who either have a physical impairment or do not have the technological literacy to be able to access the programme can do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The ability for people to pick up these skills is really quite significant.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I mean, what has become cutting-edge in a couple of years has become very normal and, in that transition, we have to make sure that there are no groups left behind in terms of accessing what has become essential services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is not one strategy; the idea of this digital inclusion and access is pervasive throughout many of our Smart Nation programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It is an event basically to engage our seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I hope maybe one day we can invite Mr Zaqy to attend one of these sessions to see how we have been able to enthuse the elderly generation to become comfortable with technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: They have learnt how to use Skype, they have learnt how to use email and they even learned how to do online banking, just from their mobile devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This is a good start to make sure that no group is left behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ultimately, this cannot just be the effort of IDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The community has to come in and, as mentioned by Minister of State Janil, that boot camp was an inter-generational effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Recently, the People’s Association has launched a whole series of courses available at many, many community centres to encourage the elderly to pick up IT skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will roll out programmes but we also need partners to work together with IDA to make sure that this becomes a reality.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Likewise, Mr Png may be aware that Okto today shows arts programmes and local productions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is something which we are also happy to discuss with Mediacorp and other players to see whether we can use the channels to be able to give opportunities to our young people to showcase their talent.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Importantly, we have to think beyond free-to-air TV because there are many possible channels to encourage arts and sports, whether it is through community events or online platforms like Toggle, which I think will appeal to our younger viewers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are different possibilities that we will explore and discuss.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And special thanks to the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPCs) as well as all Members who put in their cuts today for making this a lively discussion.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, on behalf of the GPC, I wish the Ministry all the best in the execution of the Budget and may this further our nation to its next phase of development and transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, Mdm Chair, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment. 3.15 pm
